scenes.text: It's March 12th, 1932, and you're alone in your Paris apartment.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: They call you the Match King. You make about three of every four matches on Earth.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: You've lent money to entire countries. France. Germany. Poland.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: And this morning, you know something nobody else knows yet.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: Hundreds of millions of dollars in your empire don't exist.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: Within weeks, it will be the biggest corporate collapse anyone has ever seen.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: By the end, you'll know the one money rule that got you here, and whether it still works today.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But to get here, we have to go back. It's 1880, and you're born in Kalmar, Sweden.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Your name is Ivar Kreuger. Keep count of two things: the money, and the lies.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Your family owns small match factories. The whole house smells of pine and sulfur.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Matches are cheap, but everybody needs them, every single day.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Sweden is famous for them. A Swedish inventor made the safety match popular in the 1850s.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Strike it on the box, not on your boot. Fewer fires, more sales.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Your father's factories are small, though. A few dozen workers, a lot of competition.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: Every town seems to have its own little match maker, all cutting prices.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: A billion tiny sales add up to a lot of money. Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: small match factory in Kalmar, Sweden, 1890s: wooden workbenches with piles of matchsticks, stacks of matchboxes, pine logs, a brick chimney through the window

scenes.text: At school, you're brilliant at maths, and you find tests a bit beneath you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Classmates later say you sold homework answers to other boys.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Small, quiet, and already selling something.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: At sixteen, you start engineering school in Stockholm. You graduate at twenty, with two degrees.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your father wants you in the family business. You want somewhere bigger.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So you sail to America, with almost no money.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: You work as an engineer on new steel-and-concrete buildings in New York.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: At first, the work is hard to find. You take whatever engineering job comes up.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: You go home to Sweden, get bored, and come back again.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: You also work in Mexico and South Africa. Seven years of building other people's towers.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: In South Africa, you build a restaurant and a hotel. You're barely twenty-five.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: You learn a new way to build with reinforced concrete: the Kahn system.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: And you learn something about Americans. They love a fixed deadline and a confident man.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: You lie about your experience to get some of these jobs. It works.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: In 1907, you buy the rights to the concrete system for Sweden and Germany, and go home.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: construction site of a steel-and-concrete skyscraper in New York, 1903: steel beams, wooden scaffolding, cranes, cement bags, city buildings behind

scenes.text: In 1908 you start a building company in Stockholm with an engineer, Paul Toll.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your trick: you promise fixed finish dates. Late? You pay a penalty. Early? You get a bonus.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Nobody in Europe does that. Clients love it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You build a stadium for the 1912 Stockholm Olympics. And you finish on time.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Kreuger and Toll is now a famous name. You're thirty-two.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But building houses is slow money. You want fast money.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You look at your family's little match factories, and you see a monopoly.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You merge your family's match factories in 1913, and then the whole Swedish industry.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: In 1917 it becomes Swedish Match, and you own about half of it.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Remember the billion tiny sales? Now they're yours.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: You buy match factories in country after country. Then you close the competition.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Your biggest Swedish rival holds out until 1917. Then it merges with you too.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: You standardize everything: the wood, the chemicals, the size of the box.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Fewer factories, cheaper matches, much bigger profits.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Your workers are mostly young women, packing millions of boxes a day.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: To them, you're a name on the wall. To the world, you're about to become a legend.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Where you can't buy a factory, you try to buy a law instead.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: By the late 1920s, you control between two thirds and three quarters of the world's matches.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: big Swedish match factory floor, 1915: long machines feeding matchsticks, conveyor belts, mountains of matchboxes, workers' aprons on hooks, skylights

scenes.text: You build a headquarters in Stockholm, so grand people call it the Match Palace.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: Kings, bankers and journalists come to see it, and to see you.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: You speak softly, never raise your voice, and remember every number.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: Gold mosaics. A fountain. Your office has a fake telephone.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: During meetings, an assistant rings it, and you take calls from imaginary prime ministers.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: Visitors are very impressed. That's the point.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: Remember the lie that got you jobs in America? It's a whole department now.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the Match Palace headquarters in Stockholm, 1928: grand marble hall, golden mosaics, a fountain, a huge polished desk, tall windows

scenes.text: Let's pause and look at how your empire actually works.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Imagine a set of nesting boxes, each one a company.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Box A owns Box B. Box B lends to Box C. Box C owns part of Box A.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Money can move between the boxes, and each box can report a profit from it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But from outside, you only see the lid of the biggest box.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Accountants call debts kept outside the main company off-balance-sheet.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You set up hundreds of companies, in Sweden, Liechtenstein, the Netherlands, America.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: If one box is empty, you just move money in from another box before anyone looks.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It works, as long as nobody opens all the boxes on the same day.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And you're the only person who knows what's in all the boxes.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your partners don't. Your auditors don't. Your investors certainly don't.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Remember that.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1923 you start International Match Corporation in America, and sell its shares on Wall Street.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your companies pay huge dividends. Kreuger and Toll pays twenty-five percent a year, sometimes more.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Investors love the dividends. They don't ask where they come from.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Partly, they come from new money raised from the investors themselves.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You invent new kinds of shares too, ones with almost no voting power.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So people give you money, and you keep total control.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You sell gold-backed bonds that can turn into shares. Investors line up.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You sell American certificates for your Swedish shares, so Americans can buy you too.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your financial ideas are clever. Some of them are still used today.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Time magazine puts you on its cover in October 1929.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A few days later, Wall Street crashes. And you keep paying dividends.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You look like the only safe man in finance.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Now for your boldest idea: lending money to entire countries.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: After the war, Europe is broke. Governments can't borrow anywhere.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: You offer them loans. In return, they give you a monopoly on matches.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: In 1927, France gets seventy-five million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: In 1929, Germany gets one hundred and twenty-five million.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: Remember buying a law instead of a factory? This is it. Germany's match monopoly is yours.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: That German monopoly lasts so long that it only ends in 1983.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: Poland, Hungary, Romania, Yugoslavia, and more. Fifteen countries in total.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: By 1930, you've lent governments about three hundred and eighty-seven million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: German Finance Ministry meeting hall in Berlin, 1929: long oak conference table, leather chairs, portraits, heavy curtains, a fountain pen and contracts

scenes.text: Newspapers call you the Saviour of Europe.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But here's the catch. You borrow most of that money first, from investors.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The loans pay you back slowly. Your investors expect dividends now.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The gap between those two speeds is about to swallow you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1930, President Herbert Hoover invites you to the White House.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: He wants your advice on the world economy.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: That June, a university gives you an honorary doctorate in business.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: Newspapers report you're worth more than any man in Europe. Nobody can check.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: You're probably the most trusted businessman in the world.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: The day your empire collapses is less than two years away.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: the White House Oval Office in 1930: big wooden desk, flags, armchairs, tall windows with curtains, a fireplace

scenes.text: You spend summers on your private island near Stockholm.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: Guests arrive by boat for long dinners. You hardly eat, and leave early to work.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: One of your yachts can go faster than fifty knots. You rarely have time to ride it.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: You own fast motor yachts, and apartments in Stockholm, New York, Paris and Warsaw.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: For years, a woman named Ingeborg Eberth is your companion. You never marry her.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: You never marry anyone. You barely talk about yourself at all.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: Your friends say you sleep very little, and almost never relax.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: Your old friend Krister Littorin helps run the business. He trusts you completely.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

scenes.text: Asked once about his success, Kreuger said it was built on the foolishness of people.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: private summer island villa near Stockholm, 1930: white wooden house, pine trees, a wooden jetty with a fast motor yacht, calm blue water

quote.text: I built my enterprise on the foolishness of people.

scenes.text: After the crash, the money stops coming in. The dividends don't stop going out.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You need more money every month just to keep paying.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: So, in secret, you create Italian government bonds that Italy never issued.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You design them yourself, and sign the officials' names. Some names are misspelled.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: On paper, they're worth more than one hundred million dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You use them to show your companies have assets they don't have.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: Remember the boxes? This is what's in one of them.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You also borrow from one of your companies to prop up another.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You're running faster and faster just to stand still.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You gamble on markets too, trying to win it all back. You lose tens of millions.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: You stop sleeping. Your friends notice you forgetting things, staring into space.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: Nobody asks to see the boxes. You've trained them not to.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: locked private study at night, 1930: desk lamp, sheets of blank bond paper, inkwells, a magnifying glass, rubber stamps, dark wood paneling

scenes.text: In 1931, an American company agrees to buy your Swedish phone company, Ericsson.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Its accountants check the books before paying. Most of your partners never did.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: They find that cash you claimed is missing, replaced by your own IOUs.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The deal is off. You have to pay back the money. You don't have it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You ask the Swedish central bank for a big emergency loan.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The bank says yes, if it can see all your accounts first.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Nobody has ever seen all your accounts. Not even Littorin.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In New York, you can't find the money anywhere. The banks are broke too.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You need more than ten million dollars in a few weeks, just for payments.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You sail to New York, then back to Europe. You arrive in Paris on March 11th.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: That same afternoon, you buy a pistol.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey afternoon light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: You write letters to your family and friends.

quote.text: I have made such a mess of things that I believe this is the best solution.

scenes.text: That morning, you shoot yourself. You're fifty-two.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.bgIdea: elegant Paris apartment bedroom, 1932: tall windows with grey morning light, an unmade bed, a writing desk with letters, dark wood wardrobe, Art Deco lamp

scenes.text: Your death makes front pages around the world.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then the accountants open all the boxes.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: About two hundred and fifty million dollars in assets turn out not to exist.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The manipulations were so childish anyone with basic bookkeeping should have seen them.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Thousands of ordinary investors lose their savings.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Kreuger and Toll was the most traded stock in the world. Now it's paper.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In Stockholm, the stock exchange closes for a week to stop the panic.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Littorin and the other directors are put on trial. They swear they knew nothing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The scary part is that they're probably telling the truth.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Lenders get back about forty-three cents on the dollar. Shareholders get almost nothing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The internet says you were murdered, and the scandal was framed on a dead man.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your brother wrote a whole book saying so. The police found it was suicide.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Even if someone else pulled the trigger, the fake bonds were real. Well, really fake.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And there's a second myth: that you were a genius who just had bad luck in the crash.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The crash exposed the hole. You dug it years earlier.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In 1933 and 1934, America passes new laws forcing companies to publish audited accounts.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your collapse is one of the big reasons why.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Later, the economist John Kenneth Galbraith writes about you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He calls you the Leonardo of their craft: the greatest of all swindlers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So how does the most trusted businessman in the world end up alone in Paris?
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He paid out money he didn't earn, to look like a man who never fails.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And he made sure nobody could check.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: That brings us to today's money rule.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: MONEY RULE: NO AUDIT, NO TRUST

scenes.bgIdea: modern bank branch, 2020s

scenes.text: Before you trust a company with your money, ask who checked its numbers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Here's a modern example. In August 2000, Enron shares traded at about ninety dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By December 2001, after its hidden debts came out, they were worth under one dollar.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Like your boxes, Enron hid debts in side companies most investors never looked at.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A ten thousand dollar investment at the top was worth about a hundred dollars.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So read the auditor's report, and be suspicious of profits nobody can explain.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And the rule isn't perfect. Enron had famous auditors too. They got it wrong.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: An audit lowers the risk. It doesn't remove it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So spread your money out. Never let one company hold all your savings.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Kreuger's investors trusted one man. That was the real risk.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The brightest flame can be the one that burns the house down.
scenes.speaker: narrator

meta.thumbnail: A grand 1920s marble office with towers of matchboxes and a burning match; text: 'THE MATCH KING'
meta.description:
It's 1932. You make three of every four matches on Earth and you've lent money to entire countries.
This morning, you know hundreds of millions of it don't exist. This is the life of Ivar Kreuger.

A comedic dramatization of documented history.
This video discusses suicide. If you are struggling, in the US you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline); elsewhere, contact your local emergency or crisis line.
General education only, not financial advice.

Sources:
- Ivar Kreuger, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivar_Kreuger
- Frank Partnoy, The Match King (2009)
- John Kenneth Galbraith, The Great Crash, 1929 (1954)
- Enron scandal, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enron_scandal
factCheck: Born 2 March 1880 in Kalmar, son of match industrialist Ernst August Kreuger; engineering degrees from the Royal Institute of Technology at 20 (Wikipedia).
Selling homework answers at school: Partnoy (2009), anecdotal, DISPUTED.

About seven years abroad, mostly the US, also Mexico and South Africa; Kahn system of reinforced concrete; 1907 representation rights for Sweden and Germany (Wikipedia). Exaggerating his experience to get jobs: Partnoy, DISPUTED.
Kreuger & Toll founded May 1908 with Paul Toll; fixed completion dates with penalties and bonuses (Wikipedia). Built the Stockholm Olympic Stadium for 1912 (Kreuger & Toll; widely cited).
Family factories merged 1912; Swedish combine 1913; Swedish Match 1917, Kreuger owning about half (Wikipedia). Jonkoping was a centre of Swedish match making.
Controlled two-thirds to three-quarters of world match production; International Match Corporation 1923 (Wikipedia).
Match Palace (Tandstickspalatset) completed 1928; fake telephone anecdote (Partnoy; widely cited, DISPUTED).
About 200 (other sources 400) companies; off-balance-sheet entities; B-shares; Kreuger & Toll paid 15% dividends (Wikipedia).
Time magazine cover 28 October 1929; Wall Street crash 28-29 October 1929.
Loans for match monopolies: France 1927 $75m; Germany 1929 $125m; total to foreign states about $387m by 1930; 'Saviour of Europe' (Wikipedia). 15 countries: commonly cited (Partnoy).
White House visit and Syracuse honorary doctorate, June 1930; island Angsholmen; yachts; apartments in Stockholm, New York, Paris, Warsaw; companion Ingeborg Eberth; never married (Wikipedia).
'The foolishness of people' quote: reported Kreuger remark (Wikipedia); exact wording DISPUTED.
Forged Italian government bonds, 42 bonds of 500,000 pounds each, about $142 million face value (Partnoy 2009; widely cited). Script says 'more than one hundred million'.
1931 sale of Ericsson control to ITT; ITT's audit found missing cash replaced by Kreuger IOUs; deal cancelled (Partnoy; widely cited).

February 1932 Riksbank loan request requiring full accounts; arrived Paris 11 March, found dead 12 March 1932, shot himself; letter to Littorin: 'I have made such a mess of things that I believe this to be the most satisfactory solution for everybody concerned' (Wikipedia). Script quote shortened.

About $250m claimed assets non-existent; creditors recovered about 43%; Price Waterhouse called the manipulations 'so childish' (Wikipedia). Script quote paraphrased in narration; bubble is a shortened paraphrase: DISPUTED.
Murder theory from brother Torsten Kreuger's 1965 book; police concluded suicide (Wikipedia).
Securities Acts of 1933 and 1934 heavily influenced by his collapse; Galbraith called him 'the Leonardo of their craft' in The Great Crash, 1929 (Wikipedia).
Enron traded near $90 in August 2000 and below $1 by late November-December 2001; hidden debts in special purpose entities; auditor Arthur Andersen (Wikipedia, Enron scandal).
sources: 'I built my enterprise on the foolishness of people.': Kreuger remark as reported on Wikipedia (wording varies)
'I have made such a mess of things that I believe this is the best solution.': shortened from Kreuger's letter to Krister Littorin, 12 March 1932 (Wikipedia)
'So childish.': Price Waterhouse report on Kreuger & Toll, 1932, as quoted on Wikipedia
Frank Partnoy, The Match King: Ivar Kreuger, the Financial Genius Behind a Century of Wall Street Scandals (2009)
'The Leonardo of their craft.': John Kenneth Galbraith on Kreuger, The Great Crash, 1929 (1954), as quoted on Wikipedia
